subject: computer-science
title: Functional Programming: Pure Functions
welcome_lead: Functions as the unit of composition — and no hidden state.
meta_desc: A-Level CS: pure functions, immutability and side effects.
final_note: Purity makes code easier to test and parallelise.

concepts.def: A function whose output depends only on its arguments and which causes no side effects, so the same input always yields the same output.
The principle that data values are never modified after creation; operations return new values instead of changing existing ones.
Functions treated as values: they can be stored in variables, passed as arguments and returned as results.
A function that takes one or more functions as arguments, returns a function, or both - the basis of map, filter and fold.
Map applies a function to every element of a list, returning the results; filter keeps only the elements for which a predicate is true.
A higher-order function that combines all the elements of a list into a single value by repeatedly applying a combining function.

walkthroughs.body_html: A pure function depends only on its arguments and produces no observable change beyond returning a value. add(2,3) is pure; print(x) is not. Purity gives referential transparency.
In functional code, data is immutable. To 'update' a list you create a new one. Persistent data structures share unchanged parts so this is cheaper than it sounds.
First-class functions can be stored in variables, passed as arguments and returned from other functions. Lambdas are anonymous functions used inline, e.g. x => x*2.

mcqs.q: Does map change the original list?
options: No - in functional programming data is immutable: map returns a NEW list of results and the original list is left untouched.
Yes - global variables are automatically constants in functional languages.
Yes - map deletes the original list once it has been read.
Yes - map updates each element of the original list in place.

mcqs.q: Can a pure function read and use a global variable that other code modifies?
options: Yes - map deletes the original list once it has been read.
Yes - global variables are automatically constants in functional languages.
No - if its result depends on changeable external state, the same input could give different outputs, so the function is no longer pure.
Yes - purity only forbids printing to the screen.

mcqs.q: Does filter transform each element of a list?
options: Yes - global variables are automatically constants in functional languages.
Yes - filter changes every element using its function.
Yes - filter and map are two names for the same operation.
No - filter selects elements, keeping those that satisfy the predicate unchanged; transforming each element is map's job.
